item.title: Country diary: Slugs? Dull? This one is pure showbiz | Charlie Elder
item.description:
Along the rocky shores of Falmouth, Cornwall, a tiny creature is stealing the show — and challenging every dull assumption about slugs. The rainbow sea slug, a dazzling marine species typically found off the coasts of Spain and Portugal, has been making its way north with warming seas. First spotted in UK waters near the Isles of Scilly in 2022, it has now established itself in southern bays of Cornwall and Devon, delighting citizen scientists and rockpool enthusiasts alike.
Measuring just a couple of centimeters, this flamboyant nudibranch looks almost artificial with its vivid pink body, blue finger-like projections called cerata, and yellow-orange tips — a pop-art palette that warns predators of its unpalatability. During a community "bioblitz" organized by the Rock Pool Project, the discovery of one curled beneath a submerged rock drew an admiring crowd. Marine biologist Ellie Maynard noted the species' rapid population growth, having seen over twenty individuals since her first encounter last Christmas. The slug was found beside white circles of freshly laid eggs, a sign that these sensational creatures are settling in for the long term.
This story is a quiet reminder that climate change isn't only about loss — it also brings the unexpected and extraordinary to our doorsteps. The rainbow sea slug, along with other newcomers like the aptly named hair curler slug, transforms ordinary tide-pool surveys into moments of wonder. It's a celebration of nature's capacity to surprise us, even in something as humble as a slug.

item.title: Wellington social housing sale: Living there 'changed my life' councillor says
item.description:
A Wellington city councillor has shared his personal connection to a block of social housing units now at the center of a controversial sale decision. Nureddin Abdurahman lived with his family in the Strathmore flats between 2010 and 2017 after arriving from Ethiopia, working night shifts as a taxi driver while studying at Victoria University. The affordable housing allowed him to focus on education rather than rent, eventually earning a master's degree and launching a career in politics. He recalls the deep bonds formed with neighbors who became like family, sharing food and checking on each other during hard times.
The state housing agency Kāinga Ora's decision to sell the Nuku Street properties has sparked protests and political pushback, with eleven Labour and Green councillors signing a letter questioning why homes would be sold while hundreds sleep rough on Wellington's streets. The properties themselves show significant deterioration—mould, peeling paint, and rainwater pooling inside—which Kāinga Ora cites as evidence that redevelopment isn't financially viable. Not all councillors agree with the opposition; some argue the council should focus on upgrading its own substandard housing portfolio rather than weighing in on state housing decisions.
This story captures a broader tension in housing policy: whether to preserve affordable options in their current form or seek alternatives when buildings deteriorate. What makes it quietly remarkable is hearing directly from someone whose life trajectory changed because such housing existed when he needed it most—a reminder that policy decisions play out in individual lives, shaping futures in ways that ripple forward for years.

item.title: Almost all shallow-water coral reefs now face extinction risk, study warns
item.description:
The International Union for Conservation of Nature has issued a sobering assessment of the world's coral reefs, finding that 96 percent of shallow-water coral systems now face the highest level of extinction risk. The report, released at the UN's biodiversity summit in Armenia, warns that without significant intervention, total extinction could occur by 2075. The evaluation examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems spanning more than 188,000 square kilometers, using climate projections that anticipate global temperatures rising 2.7°C above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century.
Corals are particularly vulnerable to warming oceans, which trigger damaging bleaching events with increasing frequency and intensity. When reefs collapse, the vibrant hard corals that form their foundation disappear, replaced by algae, rubble, and sponges. This transformation decimates the diverse ecosystems that depend on healthy reefs, from tiny invertebrates to commercially important fish species. The world's most celebrated reef systems—including Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle, and the Red Sea reefs—are all classified as critically endangered. The timing is especially precarious, as the emergence of a strong El Niño pattern compounds the climate-related threats these ecosystems already face.
Yet amid the stark warnings, scientists emphasize that coral reefs have demonstrated surprising resilience, with the ability to recover from severe bleaching when conditions allow. The assessment reminds us that these "rainforests of the sea" support a quarter of all marine species and provide essential resources—food, tourism revenue, and coastal protection—to communities worldwide. This story matters because it frames a critical moment: coral reefs are not yet lost, but the window for meaningful action is rapidly closing.

item.title: 'Pink man' fights for better cancer care in regions
item.description:
In the small Queensland town of Kilcoy, 85-year-old Harold Alford has become a local legend for wearing pink every single day — from his Akubra hat to his gumboots, scooter, and even his walking frame. The tradition began 25 years ago after his wife Gladys died of breast cancer on their 44th wedding anniversary, following eight grueling years of treatment that included daily trips to Brisbane for radiation. Harold chose pink as a tribute and a way to break the silence around a disease that was once considered taboo in everyday Australian conversation.
Cancer has shadowed Harold's entire life: his father died from bone cancer more than 60 years ago, and his daughter has been fighting colon and lung cancer for a decade. Now Harold himself faces a terminal lung cancer diagnosis, given 12 months to live last December. True to his character, he's opted out of treatment, preferring to "get out there and live" rather than endure debilitating chemotherapy. What began as one man's quiet tribute has grown into a town-wide movement. Through Pink Up Kilcoy, the community has raised around $30,000 for McGrath Foundation cancer care nurses, who provide free support to patients and families across regional Australia.
This story matters because it shows how personal grief can transform into collective action. Harold's willingness to wear a "stereotypically feminine" color in rural Australia — enduring ridicule until people understood his mission — helped open conversations that were once uncomfortable. In a country where nearly one in two people will be diagnosed with cancer, his gentle persistence reminds us that awareness, compassion, and community support can be as vital as medical treatment itself.

item.title: Images are all this community has left of their ancestral villages
item.description:
In Parramatta, Sydney, members of the southern Lebanese community gathered for a poignant event called The Villages We Carry, bringing photographs and videos of ancestral villages now largely destroyed. Recent analysis shows that 48 of 60 villages in occupied southern Lebanon have been mostly leveled during the conflict between Israeli forces and Hezbollah. For many Australians with Lebanese heritage, these images represent the only tangible connection to places they once called home.
Saber Serhan shared photographs from a 2000 trip to his family's village of Kfar Kila, showing his father harvesting vegetables in fields that no longer exist. Amani Haydar brought a picture of her uncle Hussam standing proudly before his shop in Aitaroun—a shop since reduced to rubble. Curator Zeinab Mahfoud is building a digital archive to preserve these memories for a community shaped by war and displacement. "Since mass migration from southern Lebanon, we've lost that connection," she explained, noting how photographs help bridge that gap across generations.
This story matters because it captures how communities preserve identity and belonging when physical places disappear. Beyond nostalgia, the archive serves as both witness and healing, allowing people to grieve losses from afar while maintaining hope for return and rebuilding. It's a quiet testament to resilience—how a collection of images can carry forward not just memory, but also the determination to pass something essential to the next generation, even when the landscape itself has been transformed beyond recognition.
